title: Lot chooses the plain (Genesis 13)
hookLine: Abram lets his nephew pick first, and Lot picks what looks best

lines: TWO BEDROOMS, ONE WITH A VIEW.
cards: Two families share a vacation rental. There are two bedrooms: one with a sea view and a big bed, one by the laundry room with bunks. Somebody has to choose.

Abram and his nephew Lot have a bigger version of that problem. They've both done well, with so many sheep, goats and cattle that the land can't feed them all, and their herdsmen have started quarreling.
Abram is the older one, the head of the family. The choice is his to make. And he doesn't make it.

teach.b: Here's what Abram says, in the King James Bible: "Let there be no strife, I pray thee, between me and thee, and between my herdmen and thy herdmen; for we be brethren." We're family.

Then: "Is not the whole land before thee? separate thyself, I pray thee, from me: if thou wilt take the left hand, then I will go to the right; or if thou depart to the right hand, then I will go to the left."

teach.h: THE OLDER LETS THE YOUNGER CHOOSE.
teach.b: The older man, the one with every right to choose first, hands the choice to the younger. And Lot looks. He "lifted up his eyes, and beheld all the plain of Jordan, that it was well watered every where."
The text compares it to the garden of the LORD. Green, rich, easy: the obvious choice, and he takes it.
The Hebrew word for that plain, kikkar, means something round: a circle of land, the same word used for a round loaf, and for a talent, that heavy round weight of silver from the parable.

But then the text adds a quiet warning: Lot pitched his tent toward Sodom, and "the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners before the LORD exceedingly." Choosing by what looks best has a cost the eyes can't see yet.
And Abram, left with the hill country? Right after Lot leaves, God tells him: lift up your eyes. Look north, south, east and west.
All of it, to you and your children.

teach.h: IS NOT THE WHOLE LAND BEFORE THEE?
teach.b: Lot lifted his eyes and grabbed. Abram is told to lift his and receive. The text doesn't call Lot a villain; he's family, and he'll be rescued more than once.
But it lets you see two ways of choosing.

how: Some Christians read Abram's choice as a picture of peacemaking and humility, and his words 'let there be no strife… for we be brethren' are quoted when families or churches work through disputes.

o: the hill country Abram kept for himself
a walled city on the plain near Sodom
a round thing: the circle of the Jordan plain

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: a round thing: plain, loaf, talent

s: as the elder, Abram chooses the best land for himself
he hands the choice to Lot: "is not the whole land before thee?"
the text compares the plain Lot chose to the garden of the LORD
after Lot leaves, God tells Abram to lift up his eyes
look north, south, east and west: Lot grabbed; Abram receives.

games.q: you're Abram, the elder. your herders and your nephew's are quarreling. the land can't hold you both. what do you do?
o: take the best land; you're the head of the family.
let Lot choose first, and take what's left.
games.why: "if thou wilt take the left hand, then I will go to the right." the one with every right to choose hands it over.

practice: Think about a small choice coming up, the last slice, the seat in the car, the parking space, where you'd normally choose first, and imagine handing it over.
Notice what you feel, relief, a twinge of loss, a little pride, and whether anything is actually at risk. If you pray, you can ask for an open hand.

wordCard.voice: Kikkar. The Hebrew word for the round, well-watered plain Lot chose at a glance, pitching his tent toward Sodom.

orig.note: Hebrew: a round thing, the circle of the Jordan plain, a round loaf, and a talent weight.

carryVoice: Your line: you choose first. An open hand has room to receive. Day three hundred forty-nine, done.
